medical.title: The invisible performance of 'masking' ADHD symptoms is exhausting
medical.summary: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is often discussed in terms of visible traits: fidgeting, distractibility, forgetfulness or restlessness. But those are just the traits we can see.

medical.title: How the visual cortex wires itself—targeted from the start, refined over time
medical.summary: A new study led by biologists at the University of California, Santa Cruz, reveals how the primary visual cortex establishes its complex long-range neural networks during early brain development. The study presents a comprehensive, fine-grained map of how the primary visual cortex connects to 11 higher visual areas during development.

medical.title: One in eight cancers are likely caused by an infection worldwide, new study finds
medical.summary: Around 12% of the world's cancer cases in 2024 were likely caused by an infection, according to new research from the World Health Organization (WHO). The study, published today in The Lancet Oncology, analyzed the frequency and causes of different cancers, specifically examining the role of infections.

medical.title: Exercise before surgery improves outcomes and shortens recovery time—new research
medical.summary: Globally, about two in three people will need major surgery at some point in their lives.

medical.title: Weapons worsen psychological harm in survivors of intimate partner violence, study finds
medical.summary: The use or threat of guns and other weapons in intimate partner violence (IPV) is associated with higher levels of panic disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms in women, new research from UNSW Sydney has found.

medical.title: Brain activity varies with age in children with autistic traits
medical.summary: Children with more autistic traits view and experience the world differently than their peers do, and those differences change as the children grow, according to a new study from WashU Medicine published Aug. 12 in the American Journal of Psychiatry. The team studied brain scans from 545 children ages 5 to 15 taken while they watched a 10-minute clip of the animated movie "Despicable Me" inside an MRI machine.

medical.title: Distinct gut microbiome patterns found in five cancer groups and in early-onset cancers
medical.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have discovered distinct gut microbiome patterns in adults 50 or younger with colorectal and breast cancers compared with those diagnosed later in life—one of several findings from an analysis of stool samples from 1,364 patients across cancer types, stages and treatments. The study is published in Cell.

medical.title: First national estimate identifies nearly 110,000 medical cannabis caregivers
medical.summary: A national analysis found that the number of clinicians authorized to approve medical cannabis use in the United States increased to more than 35,000 in 2024. The study also provides the first nationwide estimate of medical cannabis caregivers, identifying nearly 110,000 individuals who help patients obtain, grow or manage cannabis products. Caregivers outnumbered authorizing clinicians by roughly 3 to 1, highlighting the significant role they play in supporting medical cannabis use. The findings are published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

medical.title: Menthol enhances the strength and duration of nicotine's effects in rats
medical.summary: Menthol, a common flavoring for traditional cigarettes and e-cigarettes, may do more than change how nicotine tastes or feels. New research published in ACS Chemical Neuroscience reports that male rats exposed to menthol-containing e-cigarette aerosols experienced nicotine's effects more strongly and for longer than rats exposed to nicotine alone. The findings provide insight into how menthol can modify the effects of inhaled nicotine.

medical.title: Q&A: What are ultra-processed foods?
medical.summary: Nearly every day, there's a headline about ultra-processed foods, which have been linked to harmful health effects despite lacking a universally accepted definition. These foods are the subject of numerous proposed regulations, but they are not easy for consumers to avoid because they are common and often cheaper and more convenient than healthier alternatives.

medical.title: Cutting calories sheds weight initially, but body changes can drive regain
medical.summary: In the last few years, there's been a lot of interest in calorie-restricted diets for weight loss.

medical.title: EU launches first Screening Week to help detect heart and diabetes risks earlier
medical.summary: At a press conference at the EASD Annual Meeting in Milan, organized by the European Diabetes Forum (EUDF), three leading European cardiometabolic scientific associations—the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO)—joined European Commissioner for Health and Animal Welfare Olivér Várhelyi to welcome the launch of the first EU Screening Week.

medical.title: Why men face higher cancer risks may depend on the country they live in
medical.summary: Men bear a disproportionately higher burden of cancer even for cancers that are not specific to either sex. Although this pattern is global, the reasons for this difference remain mysterious. A recent study set out to investigate how much of this male-female cancer gap is solely rooted in biology and how much modifiable lifestyle habits and health conditions across populations play a role in driving it.

medical.title: Medical cannabis enrollment surged nationwide over past decade, but leveled off as recreational access expanded
medical.summary: A national analysis of medical cannabis registry data found that the number of Americans registered to use medical cannabis increased from about 747,000 in 2016 to about 3.9 million in 2024.

medical.title: Mediterranean diet linked to lower likelihood of acne in adults
medical.summary: According to new research from King's College London, adults who followed a Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and healthy fats were less likely to report acne, particularly women. In men, diets lower in carbohydrates and higher in animal-based foods were linked to a greater likelihood of acne.

medical.title: A new era of discovery for immunology: Expert Q& A
medical.summary: When two people become ill at the same time, they often experience different symptoms. For instance, during the COVID-19 pandemic, some people had symptoms akin to a mild flu, while others were critically ill. Similarly, people with chronic diseases can have very different disease courses and responses to treatment.

medical.title: How do Denmark and the UK compare when it comes to alcohol and drinking habits?
medical.summary: For decades, Denmark and the UK have been known as countries where alcohol plays a big role in people's social lives. The two countries make an interesting comparison because both have strong drinking cultures.

medical.title: Major trial examines sugar-free sweetened soft drinks
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Liverpool have conducted the longest and most comprehensive randomized controlled trial of non-nutritive sweetened (NNS) soft drinks.

medical.title: New antibodies could lead to first monoclonal treatment for measles
medical.summary: Vanderbilt Health researchers and colleagues have isolated human monoclonal antibodies from previously infected individuals that potently neutralized the measles virus in the laboratory and strongly inhibited viral replication in two animal models.

medical.title: Balancing sport with rest and work may support young athletes' mental health
medical.summary: No matter how much young athletes love their sport, they remain vulnerable to mental health and well-being problems if they don't balance the demands of training with education, work, leisure and rest.

medical.title: Loneliness and a desire to be thinner may help explain higher rates of depressive symptoms in adolescent girls
medical.summary: Adolescence, the critical developmental stage between childhood and adulthood, is often marked by significant changes in friendships, appearance, preferences and attitudes. For some young people, it can be a tumultuous period accompanied by substantial emotional distress.

medical.title: Research shows promising results for health care professionals using ketogenic diet therapy to treat mental illness
medical.summary: Specialized high-fat, low-carbohydrate diets, known as ketogenic metabolic therapy, are showing promise as treatments for certain mental illnesses in emerging research.

medical.title: Nutrition with a mission
medical.summary: After working at Telstra for 10 years, Ellie Dunlop wanted a career change.

medical.title: Researchers suggest tile-based radiation therapy as standard of care to lower risk of recurrence in brain metastases
medical.summary: A multicenter clinical trial led by researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center found that implanting collagen tiles during brain surgery to deliver targeted radiation therapy improved tumor control, lowered the risk of recurrence and improved overall survival compared with the current standard of care for patients with newly diagnosed brain metastases who need surgery.

medical.title: Hidden stem cells may be fueling spinal stenosis
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a stem cell that appears to serve as a master source for tendon and ligament cells throughout the body. In lumbar spinal stenosis, these cells become unusually active and may drive the ligament overgrowth that squeezes spinal nerves and causes pain, numbness, and difficulty walking. Researchers found that reducing calcium signaling stopped this abnormal growth in mice.

science.title: NASA announces new missions for Boeing Starliner spacecraft

science.title: Tropical weather patterns steer West Antarctic snowfall, ice cores reveal
science.summary: Climate patterns in the tropics help determine how much snow falls from year to year in Antarctica, one of the coldest, windiest and driest places on Earth. New research from the University of Utah shows that tropical conditions and the oceans also influence the continent's massive ice sheets.

science.title: This cat is new to science. What does it take to identify a species?
science.summary: There's a new cat in town, but this one won't curl up on your hamper, knead your sweaters or squeeze in front of your screen during a Zoom meeting.

science.title: Rotating light pattern reveals laser frequency in a single image
science.summary: An international team of physicists has developed a new method for determining the precise color of laser light using an image that rotates as the laser's frequency shifts.

science.title: Scandium's electrons may explain predicted room-temperature superconductivity
science.summary: Scientists have confirmed the existence of a predicted room temperature superconductor, while explaining the microscopic mechanism that distinguishes it from a similar one discovered several years ago. The work, published in the journal Physical Review B, offers "a theoretical blueprint for the future design of superior superconductor hydrides" the physicists write.

science.title: Tokyo suffers the longest streak of rainy days on record

science.title: Identical hiring algorithms may create echo chambers that overlook stronger job candidates
science.summary: AI tools are increasingly replacing human judgments in some settings. For instance, resume-screening algorithms are often used in hiring, where they may improve efficiency and consistency in decision-making.

science.title: Study shows California's rodenticide restrictions are working, and flags new rodenticides rising in their place

science.title: India turns to corals and seagrass to shield against rising seas
science.summary: Under a blazing sun, workers crouch on a shrinking island off India's southern coast, threading bright green seagrass shoots onto wooden frames before anchoring them to the ocean floor.

science.title: Enantioresolution turns bright but racemic gold-silver clusters into circularly polarized emitters
science.summary: Chiral metal clusters that emit circularly polarized light often face a trade-off between photoluminescence efficiency and luminescence dissymmetry. A study published in the journal Advanced Optical Materials tested whether highly luminescent racemic carbon-centered gold(I)-silver(I) clusters could be converted into bright CPL emitters by enantioresolution with chiral donor ligands.

science.title: Same plant species, different chemistry: Why chemotype labels matter
science.summary: Plants of the same species can differ considerably in their chemical composition, affecting their smell, taste and even toxicity. A new study shows that the term "chemotype" has not been used consistently.

science.title: New statistical method can flag hidden anomalies in scientific datasets
science.summary: A research team at the University of Vienna, led by pharmaceutical chemist Johannes Kirchmair, has developed a statistical method to identify hidden anomalies in scientific datasets. The method can be applied automatically to large datasets, making it easier for researchers to pinpoint those that need closer scrutiny. The approach improves the quality of data-driven research and supports the development of reliable AI applications.

science.title: NASA ramps up support to get Boeing's astronaut capsule flying after Butch and Suni fiasco
science.summary: NASA is throwing extra support and money behind Boeing's troubled astronaut capsule to get it fixed and flying again as soon as possible.

science.title: Feeling like you are losing ground predicts suicidal ideation more than income or age
science.summary: New research finds that people are far more likely to report suicidal ideation when they perceive their lives as getting worse relative to their recent past, rather than because of their income, age or health status alone.

science.title: Ancient bird becomes second Australian species to be named from the Cretaceous period
science.summary: A pair of exceptionally rare Cretaceous bird bones found at separate sites near Richmond, Queensland, reveal a previously unknown species—the second formally named Cretaceous bird from Australia. Cretaceous bird fossils are extremely scarce in Australia, with fewer than a dozen isolated bones reported, making these finds especially significant. The research is published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

science.title: The molecular mechanism that regulates TMEM63B lipid scrambling
science.summary: TMEM63B, a mechanosensitive lipid scramblase, has an autoinhibitory domain in its C-terminal tail that helps keep it inactive under resting conditions, researchers from the Institute of Science Tokyo report. Changes to this regulatory region, particularly the Leu776 residue, reverse the inhibitory action and cause continuous lipid scrambling, disrupting normal phospholipid asymmetry.

science.title: Researcher solves a nanoparticle mystery using an iPhone camera
science.summary: Instead of capturing a memory with an iPhone camera, Carnegie Mellon University's Nivedita Shyamsundar used hers to make a scientific discovery. A senior in the Department of Chemistry, Shyamsundar studies tiny particles that could help medicines and vaccines travel more effectively through the human body and reach their targets. Her work may one day lead to better cancer treatments and stronger vaccines.

science.title: Half a million older Scots facing fuel insecurity, study finds
science.summary: Data from more than 4,000 adults across Scotland showed that fuel, food and financial insecurity are widespread, and more than 1 in 10 adults experience all three simultaneously.

science.title: Peeling crust beneath Italy's Apennines may explain why mountains stretch and squeeze
science.summary: Extending some 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) along the length of Italy, the Apennine Mountains present a challenging puzzle for geologists. In some places, the mountains are steadily being stretched apart, while in regions just tens of kilometers away, they are squeezing together.

science.title: How NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will open a window into the Milky Way
science.summary: Look up at the night sky with the naked eye and it may seem like it rarely changes. Yet the universe is in constant flux. Stars drift through space, orbiting the center of the Milky Way as planets orbit them. They rotate, showing spots on their surfaces and sometimes producing violent outbursts that affect planetary atmospheres much like solar storms produce auroras on Earth.

science.title: The novel on your nightstand may be doing more for your empathy and cognitive health than you think
science.summary: A popular narrative across Instagram Reels, business podcasts and magazine covers is that people who are smart and serious about growth read nonfiction. Nonfiction directly provides factual information and real-world knowledge, whereas fiction, like novels and poetry, is treated as a less practical cousin. Now, a recent study has asked whether fiction really is just entertainment.

science.title: Diving into an out-of-sync galaxy
science.summary: Galaxies are like snowflakes: No two are exactly alike, even the spirals. The Hubble Space Telescope took a close look at the distant spiral NGC 4693 and found intriguing hints about its past. For one thing, this member of the Virgo Cluster seems to have a central region that's rotating out of sync with its spiral arms and bulge. Those arms don't seem to connect to the central region, and the bulge itself seems to extend above the plane of the galaxy. In other words, there seems to be a decoupling between the arms and the bulge.

science.title: Biologists may have discovered two of the world's loudest birds
science.summary: University of Massachusetts Amherst's Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João C.T. Menezes have identified two contenders for the title of world's loudest bird: the bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema. Their findings also help explain why some birds are so much louder than others.

science.title: Perceived motives help explain why some online campaigns fail to mobilize support

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in

Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species

Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: Exercise before surgery improves outcomes and shortens recovery time—new research
mix_items.summary: Globally, about two in three people will need major surgery at some point in their lives.

mix_items.title: Scandium's electrons may explain predicted room-temperature superconductivity
mix_items.summary: Scientists have confirmed the existence of a predicted room temperature superconductor, while explaining the microscopic mechanism that distinguishes it from a similar one discovered several years ago. The work, published in the journal Physical Review B, offers "a theoretical blueprint for the future design of superior superconductor hydrides" the physicists write.

mix_items.title: Tokyo suffers the longest streak of rainy days on record
mix_items.summary: Tokyo has logged 34 straight days of rain, the longest streak on record, Japan's weather agency said Tuesday.

mix_items.title: Identical hiring algorithms may create echo chambers that overlook stronger job candidates
mix_items.summary: AI tools are increasingly replacing human judgments in some settings. For instance, resume-screening algorithms are often used in hiring, where they may improve efficiency and consistency in decision-making.

mix_items.title: Weapons worsen psychological harm in survivors of intimate partner violence, study finds
mix_items.summary: The use or threat of guns and other weapons in intimate partner violence (IPV) is associated with higher levels of panic disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms in women, new research from UNSW Sydney has found.

mix_items.title: Study shows California's rodenticide restrictions are working, and flags new rodenticides rising in their place
mix_items.summary: New research from the Integral Ecology Research Center (IERC) offers some of the clearest evidence yet that California's efforts to restrict dangerous rodenticides are paying off in the wild, while also flagging a new contaminant that deserves close attention.

mix_items.title: India turns to corals and seagrass to shield against rising seas
mix_items.summary: Under a blazing sun, workers crouch on a shrinking island off India's southern coast, threading bright green seagrass shoots onto wooden frames before anchoring them to the ocean floor.

mix_items.title: Brain activity varies with age in children with autistic traits
mix_items.summary: Children with more autistic traits view and experience the world differently than their peers do, and those differences change as the children grow, according to a new study from WashU Medicine published Aug. 12 in the American Journal of Psychiatry. The team studied brain scans from 545 children ages 5 to 15 taken while they watched a 10-minute clip of the animated movie "Despicable Me" inside an MRI machine.

mix_items.title: Enantioresolution turns bright but racemic gold-silver clusters into circularly polarized emitters
mix_items.summary: Chiral metal clusters that emit circularly polarized light often face a trade-off between photoluminescence efficiency and luminescence dissymmetry. A study published in the journal Advanced Optical Materials tested whether highly luminescent racemic carbon-centered gold(I)-silver(I) clusters could be converted into bright CPL emitters by enantioresolution with chiral donor ligands.

mix_items.title: Same plant species, different chemistry: Why chemotype labels matter
mix_items.summary: Plants of the same species can differ considerably in their chemical composition, affecting their smell, taste and even toxicity. A new study shows that the term "chemotype" has not been used consistently.

mix_items.title: New statistical method can flag hidden anomalies in scientific datasets
mix_items.summary: A research team at the University of Vienna, led by pharmaceutical chemist Johannes Kirchmair, has developed a statistical method to identify hidden anomalies in scientific datasets. The method can be applied automatically to large datasets, making it easier for researchers to pinpoint those that need closer scrutiny. The approach improves the quality of data-driven research and supports the development of reliable AI applications.

mix_items.title: Distinct gut microbiome patterns found in five cancer groups and in early-onset cancers
mix_items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have discovered distinct gut microbiome patterns in adults 50 or younger with colorectal and breast cancers compared with those diagnosed later in life—one of several findings from an analysis of stool samples from 1,364 patients across cancer types, stages and treatments. The study is published in Cell.

mix_items.title: NASA ramps up support to get Boeing's astronaut capsule flying after Butch and Suni fiasco
mix_items.summary: NASA is throwing extra support and money behind Boeing's troubled astronaut capsule to get it fixed and flying again as soon as possible.

mix_items.title: Feeling like you are losing ground predicts suicidal ideation more than income or age
mix_items.summary: New research finds that people are far more likely to report suicidal ideation when they perceive their lives as getting worse relative to their recent past, rather than because of their income, age or health status alone.

mix_items.title: First national estimate identifies nearly 110,000 medical cannabis caregivers
mix_items.summary: A national analysis found that the number of clinicians authorized to approve medical cannabis use in the United States increased to more than 35,000 in 2024. The study also provides the first nationwide estimate of medical cannabis caregivers, identifying nearly 110,000 individuals who help patients obtain, grow or manage cannabis products. Caregivers outnumbered authorizing clinicians by roughly 3 to 1, highlighting the significant role they play in supporting medical cannabis use. The findings are published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

mix_items.title: Ancient bird becomes second Australian species to be named from the Cretaceous period
mix_items.summary: A pair of exceptionally rare Cretaceous bird bones found at separate sites near Richmond, Queensland, reveal a previously unknown species—the second formally named Cretaceous bird from Australia. Cretaceous bird fossils are extremely scarce in Australia, with fewer than a dozen isolated bones reported, making these finds especially significant. The research is published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

mix_items.title: Menthol enhances the strength and duration of nicotine's effects in rats
mix_items.summary: Menthol, a common flavoring for traditional cigarettes and e-cigarettes, may do more than change how nicotine tastes or feels. New research published in ACS Chemical Neuroscience reports that male rats exposed to menthol-containing e-cigarette aerosols experienced nicotine's effects more strongly and for longer than rats exposed to nicotine alone. The findings provide insight into how menthol can modify the effects of inhaled nicotine.

mix_items.title: The molecular mechanism that regulates TMEM63B lipid scrambling
mix_items.summary: TMEM63B, a mechanosensitive lipid scramblase, has an autoinhibitory domain in its C-terminal tail that helps keep it inactive under resting conditions, researchers from the Institute of Science Tokyo report. Changes to this regulatory region, particularly the Leu776 residue, reverse the inhibitory action and cause continuous lipid scrambling, disrupting normal phospholipid asymmetry.

mix_items.title: Researcher solves a nanoparticle mystery using an iPhone camera
mix_items.summary: Instead of capturing a memory with an iPhone camera, Carnegie Mellon University's Nivedita Shyamsundar used hers to make a scientific discovery. A senior in the Department of Chemistry, Shyamsundar studies tiny particles that could help medicines and vaccines travel more effectively through the human body and reach their targets. Her work may one day lead to better cancer treatments and stronger vaccines.

mix_items.title: Q&A: What are ultra-processed foods?
mix_items.summary: Nearly every day, there's a headline about ultra-processed foods, which have been linked to harmful health effects despite lacking a universally accepted definition. These foods are the subject of numerous proposed regulations, but they are not easy for consumers to avoid because they are common and often cheaper and more convenient than healthier alternatives.

mix_items.title: Half a million older Scots facing fuel insecurity, study finds
mix_items.summary: Data from more than 4,000 adults across Scotland showed that fuel, food and financial insecurity are widespread, and more than 1 in 10 adults experience all three simultaneously.

mix_items.title: Cutting calories sheds weight initially, but body changes can drive regain
mix_items.summary: In the last few years, there's been a lot of interest in calorie-restricted diets for weight loss.

mix_items.title: EU launches first Screening Week to help detect heart and diabetes risks earlier
mix_items.summary: At a press conference at the EASD Annual Meeting in Milan, organized by the European Diabetes Forum (EUDF), three leading European cardiometabolic scientific associations—the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO)—joined European Commissioner for Health and Animal Welfare Olivér Várhelyi to welcome the launch of the first EU Screening Week.

mix_items.title: Peeling crust beneath Italy's Apennines may explain why mountains stretch and squeeze
mix_items.summary: Extending some 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) along the length of Italy, the Apennine Mountains present a challenging puzzle for geologists. In some places, the mountains are steadily being stretched apart, while in regions just tens of kilometers away, they are squeezing together.

mix_items.title: Why men face higher cancer risks may depend on the country they live in
mix_items.summary: Men bear a disproportionately higher burden of cancer even for cancers that are not specific to either sex. Although this pattern is global, the reasons for this difference remain mysterious. A recent study set out to investigate how much of this male-female cancer gap is solely rooted in biology and how much modifiable lifestyle habits and health conditions across populations play a role in driving it.

mix_items.title: Medical cannabis enrollment surged nationwide over past decade, but leveled off as recreational access expanded
mix_items.summary: A national analysis of medical cannabis registry data found that the number of Americans registered to use medical cannabis increased from about 747,000 in 2016 to about 3.9 million in 2024.

mix_items.title: How NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will open a window into the Milky Way
mix_items.summary: Look up at the night sky with the naked eye and it may seem like it rarely changes. Yet the universe is in constant flux. Stars drift through space, orbiting the center of the Milky Way as planets orbit them. They rotate, showing spots on their surfaces and sometimes producing violent outbursts that affect planetary atmospheres much like solar storms produce auroras on Earth.

mix_items.title: Mediterranean diet linked to lower likelihood of acne in adults
mix_items.summary: According to new research from King's College London, adults who followed a Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and healthy fats were less likely to report acne, particularly women. In men, diets lower in carbohydrates and higher in animal-based foods were linked to a greater likelihood of acne.

mix_items.title: The novel on your nightstand may be doing more for your empathy and cognitive health than you think
mix_items.summary: A popular narrative across Instagram Reels, business podcasts and magazine covers is that people who are smart and serious about growth read nonfiction. Nonfiction directly provides factual information and real-world knowledge, whereas fiction, like novels and poetry, is treated as a less practical cousin. Now, a recent study has asked whether fiction really is just entertainment.

mix_items.title: Diving into an out-of-sync galaxy
mix_items.summary: Galaxies are like snowflakes: No two are exactly alike, even the spirals. The Hubble Space Telescope took a close look at the distant spiral NGC 4693 and found intriguing hints about its past. For one thing, this member of the Virgo Cluster seems to have a central region that's rotating out of sync with its spiral arms and bulge. Those arms don't seem to connect to the central region, and the bulge itself seems to extend above the plane of the galaxy. In other words, there seems to be a decoupling between the arms and the bulge.

mix_items.title: A new era of discovery for immunology: Expert Q& A
mix_items.summary: When two people become ill at the same time, they often experience different symptoms. For instance, during the COVID-19 pandemic, some people had symptoms akin to a mild flu, while others were critically ill. Similarly, people with chronic diseases can have very different disease courses and responses to treatment.

mix_items.title: Biologists may have discovered two of the world's loudest birds
mix_items.summary: University of Massachusetts Amherst's Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João C.T. Menezes have identified two contenders for the title of world's loudest bird: the bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema. Their findings also help explain why some birds are so much louder than others.

mix_items.title: Nature-strip gardens boost biodiversity, bugs and social benefits
mix_items.summary: University of Melbourne researchers have found that planting native gardens on suburban nature strips can boost urban biodiversity, with insect numbers increasing sevenfold and the number of species approximately doubling.

mix_items.title: How do Denmark and the UK compare when it comes to alcohol and drinking habits?
mix_items.summary: For decades, Denmark and the UK have been known as countries where alcohol plays a big role in people's social lives. The two countries make an interesting comparison because both have strong drinking cultures.

mix_items.title: Major trial examines sugar-free sweetened soft drinks
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Liverpool have conducted the longest and most comprehensive randomized controlled trial of non-nutritive sweetened (NNS) soft drinks.

mix_items.title: Perceived motives help explain why some online campaigns fail to mobilize support
mix_items.summary: Flinders University researchers have examined the role social media plays in expanding social movements and found that perceptions of online activists' motives can significantly affect others' willingness to participate. The study is published in the journal New Media & Society.

mix_items.title: New antibodies could lead to first monoclonal treatment for measles
mix_items.summary: Vanderbilt Health researchers and colleagues have isolated human monoclonal antibodies from previously infected individuals that potently neutralized the measles virus in the laboratory and strongly inhibited viral replication in two animal models.

mix_items.title: Balancing sport with rest and work may support young athletes' mental health
mix_items.summary: No matter how much young athletes love their sport, they remain vulnerable to mental health and well-being problems if they don't balance the demands of training with education, work, leisure and rest.

mix_items.title: Loneliness and a desire to be thinner may help explain higher rates of depressive symptoms in adolescent girls
mix_items.summary: Adolescence, the critical developmental stage between childhood and adulthood, is often marked by significant changes in friendships, appearance, preferences and attitudes. For some young people, it can be a tumultuous period accompanied by substantial emotional distress.

mix_items.title: Research shows promising results for health care professionals using ketogenic diet therapy to treat mental illness
mix_items.summary: Specialized high-fat, low-carbohydrate diets, known as ketogenic metabolic therapy, are showing promise as treatments for certain mental illnesses in emerging research.

mix_items.title: Nutrition with a mission
mix_items.summary: After working at Telstra for 10 years, Ellie Dunlop wanted a career change.

mix_items.title: Researchers suggest tile-based radiation therapy as standard of care to lower risk of recurrence in brain metastases
mix_items.summary: A multicenter clinical trial led by researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center found that implanting collagen tiles during brain surgery to deliver targeted radiation therapy improved tumor control, lowered the risk of recurrence and improved overall survival compared with the current standard of care for patients with newly diagnosed brain metastases who need surgery.

mix_items.title: Hidden stem cells may be fueling spinal stenosis
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a stem cell that appears to serve as a master source for tendon and ligament cells throughout the body. In lumbar spinal stenosis, these cells become unusually active and may drive the ligament overgrowth that squeezes spinal nerves and causes pain, numbness, and difficulty walking. Researchers found that reducing calcium signaling stopped this abnormal growth in mice.

mix_items.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
mix_items.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. mix_items.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
mix_items.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. mix_items.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific
mix_items.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .
